name: Spatial landmark legibility
summary: A traversable space becomes learnable when rooms and junctions carry stable visual, audio, functional, and topological identities instead of differing only by coordinates.
player_action: The player enters, crosses, leaves, and later identifies a room or junction without relying exclusively on a waypoint.
system_response: The environment presents persistent landmarks, silhouettes, sounds, functions, and route relationships that distinguish the location from its neighbors.

weakened_by: landmarks visible only from one approach
conflicts_with: layout mutation that erases every learned relationship

failure_modes: Players identify rooms only through HUD labels.
Adjacent spaces share silhouette, lighting, props, and function.
A landmark does not help predict any route.
Procedural assembly produces technically connected but cognitively identical rooms.
accessibility: Repeat important identity through shape, sound, text, and contrast rather than color alone.
Allow map and orientation assistance without removing environmental landmarks.

smallest_playable_test.setup: One six-room loop with two branches, three junctions, and distinct landmark channels that can be toggled independently.
smallest_playable_test.retain_if: Most players can name or describe each junction and intentionally return to a chosen room from more than one approach.
smallest_playable_test.revise_if: The route is learnable but depends on one sensory channel or one viewing direction.
smallest_playable_test.reject_if: Players traverse successfully only by following markers or memorizing an arbitrary turn sequence.

evidence.claim: Nintendo developers describe adding valuable cave entrances to familiar cliffs so players reinterpret the landscape and let one hint lead to another.
evidence.game_version: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom developer interview
evidence.notes: Supports environmental differences changing route attention; it does not prove one universal landmark formula.
